opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that robotics spent a long time trying to solve every problem from scratch, inside the robot, with robot data alone. That was very expensive. Every new skill meant collecting thousands of demonstrations or running reinforcement learning for months, and what you got at the end was often brittle. It worked in one lab, on one table, with one set of objects.

What changed with internet-scale foundation models is that a huge share of what a robot needs to know isn't really about motor control at all. It's semantics. What is a sponge, where do people usually keep cups, what does "clean up the spill" actually imply, which object is the "extinct animal" on the table. That kind of common-sense, visual, and linguistic knowledge is massively represented on the internet, and language and vision-language models soak it up. So suddenly robotics can borrow that knowledge instead of trying to rediscover it through physical trial and error.

We saw this happen in a few waves. First, people used large language models as high-level planners, with work like SayCan, where the language model proposes steps and the robot's learned skills ground them in what's actually feasible. Then people started treating the robot itself as a modality. With RT-1 we showed that a transformer trained on a large, diverse robot dataset could absorb a lot of tasks at once. With RT-2 we went further: we took a vision-language model pretrained on web data and fine-tuned it to output robot actions as tokens. The interesting part was the emergent generalization. The robot could follow instructions involving concepts that never showed up in its robot data, because that knowledge was transferred from the web.

So I think the acceleration comes from three things coming together. One is transfer: priors from internet data mean you need far less robot data to get broad, flexible behavior. Two is a shared recipe: robotics can now ride the same scaling curves, architectures, and infrastructure as the rest of AI, rather than being a niche with bespoke methods. Three is a cultural shift toward pooling data. Efforts like Open X-Embodiment, where many labs combined datasets across many robot types, only make sense once you believe a single large model can benefit from heterogeneous data.

I'd also add a note of humility. Foundation models didn't solve the physical part. Low-level dexterity, contact-rich manipulation, and reliability at the long tail are still hard, and we don't have an internet of robot actions. Data remains the bottleneck. But the starting point is completely different now. Instead of building intelligence from the ground up for every robot, we're increasingly asking how to connect a very capable general model to a body, and that's a much more tractable and exciting problem.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models provide knowledge transfer, shared methods, and pooled data, but it does not explain acceleration as improved success rates across many robotics components making the whole system easier to get working.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the simplest way I'd put it is that robotics went from being a field where every single problem had to be solved from scratch, in-house, with your own data, to a field where you can finally stand on the shoulders of everything that's been built in language and vision. And that shift happened really fast.

If you rewind to, say, 2018 or 2019, the state of the art in robot learning was: you pick one task, you collect a bunch of demonstrations or run a lot of RL in simulation, you train a policy, and it works on that task, in that environment, with that robot. Maybe. And the moment you change the lighting or the object or the table height, it falls apart. There was no concept of "generalization" in the way we think about it now. The data was tiny, the models were small, and basically nothing transferred.

What foundation models did was change the premise. All of a sudden you have models that already know what a coffee mug is, what "put the mug in the sink" means, roughly what a kitchen looks like, and even some common-sense reasoning about how objects behave. All of that is knowledge the robot used to have to learn from its own experience, and now it just comes for free from internet-scale pretraining. So the robot's job shrinks from "understand the world and act in it" to "learn how to act, given that someone already handed you a pretty good understanding of the world."

And I think there are really three things that compounded. One is the knowledge transfer piece I just mentioned, which is the obvious one. Two is that the architectures converged. Once everything is a transformer taking in tokens, it stops mattering so much whether a token came from text, from an image, or from a robot's joint angles. So the same modeling tricks, the same scaling recipes, the same infrastructure that language people spent years hardening, all of that becomes directly usable. Robotics researchers could borrow instead of invent.

And the third one, which I think is underrated, is that it changed the culture and the ambition level. When you see what scaling did in language, you start asking, why wouldn't that work for us? What's our version of a web crawl? That's what drove a lot of the push toward larger, more diverse robot datasets, cross-embodiment training, these open collaborations across labs pooling data. People stopped optimizing for the single benchmark and started asking how to get a model that handles a hundred tasks it's never seen.

Now, I want to be honest that it's not a perfect analogy. The internet gave language models trillions of tokens of exactly the thing they needed to predict. There is no equivalent for robot actions. Nobody uploaded a hundred billion hours of labeled motor commands. So the bottleneck in robotics is still data, and the acceleration you're seeing is partly real capability gains and partly that we finally have a credible story for how to attack the data problem, through pretraining, through simulation, through scaling up human teleop, through video. The foundation models bought us a huge head start on perception and semantics. The "what do I actually do with my arm" part is still hard, and that's where most of the interesting work is right now.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes acceleration to transferred knowledge, shared architectures and infrastructure, and increased ambition around data. It does not say that improved success rates across multiple robotics components make it easier to get the whole system working.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that robotics is no longer having to learn everything from scratch. Traditionally, if you wanted a robot to do a task, you would collect data for that task in a particular environment and train a system that was fairly specialized. A lot of the work you put into one task didn’t necessarily carry over to the next one.

With internet-scale foundation models, you have a starting point that already contains a lot of useful structure about the world: visual representations, language understanding, and relationships between objects and activities. The question becomes: how do we connect those capabilities to a robot’s observations and actions?

That doesn’t mean an internet-trained model automatically knows how to control a robot. There’s still a substantial gap between describing how to pick something up and actually doing it reliably. You need physical interaction data, and you need to deal with things like contact, uncertainty, and recovering when something goes wrong.

But it changes the leverage you get from that robot data. Instead of using it to teach the system everything, you’re using it to connect a much richer pretrained model to physical behavior. And that opens up this possibility that improvements in models, compute, and robotics data can build on each other, rather than every new task being a separate research project.

r001.rationale: The response says pretrained capabilities and robotics data can build on each other, but does not explain that improved success rates across many robotics components make it easier to get the whole system working.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a big part of it is that robotics is starting to benefit from progress that happened outside robotics. Historically, if you wanted a robot to do a task, you had to build a lot of the perception, planning, and control machinery specifically for that task. And the data you could collect on a robot was relatively expensive and limited.

Internet-scale foundation models give us a very different starting point. A model can come in with useful representations of objects, language, and relationships in the world before it ever sees robot data. Then the question becomes: how do we connect those capabilities to physical actions?

That connection still takes real work. Understanding an instruction or recognizing an object doesn’t automatically mean you can grasp it reliably. But you’re no longer trying to learn everything from scratch. You can use robot experience to teach the parts that are specific to embodiment, while taking advantage of much broader knowledge learned elsewhere.

And that changes the research loop. You can try more tasks, get meaningful results sooner, and start investigating generalization across tasks rather than building a separate system for each one. I think that’s a major reason the field feels like it’s accelerating.

r001.rationale: The response says foundation models provide useful prior representations and let researchers get meaningful results sooner, but it does not explain that improved success rates across multiple robotics components make it easier to get the whole system working.
